questions.question:
Which of the following idioms given in the alternatives has the meaning?
An avoidable error in which something good or of value is eliminated when trying to get rid of something unwanted.

options.text: Throw the baby out with the bathwater
Lock someone up and throw away the key

questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option (2)** i.e. **'Throw the baby out with the bathwater'**.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• The meaning **'An avoidable error in which something good or of value is eliminated when trying to get rid of something unwanted'** refers to a situation where an essential or valuable part of something is discarded while attempting to remove undesirable elements. (किसी अवांछित चीज़ से छुटकारा पाने की कोशिश करते समय किसी अच्छी या मूल्यवान चीज़ को हटा देने की एक टालने योग्य गलती।)
 
 
• **Example:** Closing the entire library because a few books were missing is a classic case of **throwing the baby out with the bathwater**.
 
 
 
• The idiom **'Throw the baby out with the bathwater'** means to lose valuable ideas or things during an attempt to get rid of what is not wanted. (अवांछित चीज़ों के साथ-साथ मूल्यवान चीज़ों को भी त्याग देना।)
 
 
• **Example:** We should update our old software rather than scrapping the whole system; let us not **throw the baby out with the bathwater**.
 
 
 
• Hence, we can infer that the meaning provided in the question matches the idiom **'Throw the baby out with the bathwater'**.

Therefore, the correct answer is- **Throw the baby out with the bathwater**.

**Additional Information__**

Here are the other options explained along with their Hindi meanings and example sentences:

__
 
• **Throw somebody for a loop** (किसी को बहुत अधिक चकित या परेशान कर देना): To surprise, shock, or confuse someone significantly.
 
 
• **Example:** The news of the sudden policy change **threw the entire staff for a loop**.
 
 
 
• **Throw the first stone** (आरोप लगाने वाला पहला व्यक्ति बनना जबकि स्वयं भी निर्दोष न हो): To be the first to criticize someone for a fault that the critic also possesses.
 
 
• **Example:** Before you judge her for being messy, look at your own desk; you should not be the one to **throw the first stone**.
 
 
 
• **Lock someone up and throw away the key** (किसी को बहुत लंबे समय या आजीवन कारावास में डालना): To put someone in prison for a very long time or for life.
 
 
• **Example:** The criminal was so dangerous that many felt the judge should **lock him up and throw away the key**.

questions.question:
Select the correct alternative to fill in the blank with the correct preposition in the following sentence.
Cover your face ______ your palms to save yourself from the dust storm.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is '**with**'. **__Key Points__** __ 
• The **preposition** '**with**' is used to indicate the **instrument**, **tool**, or **part of the body** used to perform a specific action. 
• In this sentence, the **palms** are the **means** or **instruments** used to perform the action of **covering** the face. 
• The standard **grammatical colocation** for this context is **'to cover something with something'**. Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 3**. **Complete Sentence:** *'Cover your face **with**__ your palms to save yourself from the dust storm.'* **__Additional Information__** 
• **Option 1 (behind):** This preposition refers to a **location** at the **back** of something and does not fit the context of using an object to cover another. 
• **Option 2 (under):** This refers to being **directly below** or **beneath** something; one does not cover their face 'under' their palms in this active sense. </ul

questions.question:
Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into Passive Voice?
Did the technician repair the machinery before the factory resumed operations?

options.text: Was the machinery repaired by the technician before the factory resumed operations?
Was the machinery being repaired by the technician before the factory resumed operations?
Has the machinery been repaired by the technician before the factory resumed operations?
Did the machinery repair by the technician before the factory resumed operations?

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Was the machinery repaired by the technician before the factory resumed operations?**__.

**__Key Points__**

__

• The original sentence is in the **Active Voice** and follows the **Simple Past Tense** interrogative pattern: **Did + Subject + V1 + Object**.

• To convert an interrogative **Simple Past** sentence into **Passive Voice**, the auxiliary verb **Did** is replaced by **Was** or **Were** based on the number and person of the new subject.

• The word **machinery** is an **uncountable noun** and is treated as **singular**; therefore, the auxiliary verb **Was** is used to start the passive sentence.

• The main verb **repair** (V1) must be changed into its **Past Participle** form (V3), which is **repaired**.

• The agent or **Subject** of the active sentence (**the technician**) is placed after the verb, preceded by the preposition **by**.

• The **Adverbial Clause** of time, **before the factory resumed operations**, remains unchanged as it provides context to the main action.

• The final passive structure becomes: **Was + New Subject (the machinery) + V3 (repaired) + by + Agent (the technician) + remainder of the sentence**.

 **Additional Information__**

• Analysis of incorrect options:

• **Past Continuous Passive**: Option 2 uses the phrase **being repaired**, which is only used when the original active sentence is in the **Past Continuous Tense** (Was the technician repairing...).

• **Present Perfect Passive**: Option 3 uses **Has the machinery been repaired**, which shifts the tense from the **Simple Past** to the **Present Perfect**, changing the temporal meaning of the sentence.

• **Grammatical Error**: Option 4 uses **Did the machinery repair**, which is structurally incorrect because **machinery** is the receiver of the action, not the performer, necessitating a **Passive Voice** construction.

• Tense Consistency: In voice conversion, the **Tense** must remain the same; **Simple Past Active** must always correspond to **Simple Past Passive**.
</ul

questions.question:
Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into active voice?
Was the project presentation being evaluated by the panel when the power cut occurred?

options.text: Did the panel evaluate the project presentation when the power cut occurred?
Is the panel evaluating the project presentation when the power cut occurred?
Was the panel evaluating the project presentation when the power cut occurred?
Had the panel evaluated the project presentation when the power cut occurred?

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Was the panel evaluating the project presentation when the power cut occurred?**__.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• The original sentence 'Was the project presentation being evaluated by the panel when the power cut occurred?' is in the **Passive Voice** of the **Past Continuous Tense**.
 
• The structure for an **interrogative sentence** in the **Past Continuous Passive Voice** is: **Was/Were + Object + being + V3 (Past Participle) + by + Subject?**
 
• To convert this into **Active Voice**, the structure must be: **Was/Were + Subject + Verb-ing (Present Participle) + Object?**
 
• In the given sentence, the **subject** (the doer) is **the panel**, and the **object** (the receiver) is **the project presentation**. The verb is **evaluate**.
 
• Applying the rule, 'the panel' (singular subject) takes the auxiliary verb **Was**, and the verb changes from 'being evaluated' to **evaluating**.
 
• The clause 'when the power cut occurred' remains unchanged as it provides the **temporal context** (Simple Past) for the continuous action.

 **Additional Information__**

 
• Understanding **Tense Consistency** in Voice Conversion:
 
 
• **Past Simple**: Uses the auxiliary **Did** in the active interrogative (e.g., 'Did the panel evaluate...'). This is incorrect here because the original sentence denotes an **ongoing action** (indicated by 'being').
 
• **Present Continuous**: Uses **Is/Am/Are**. This is incorrect because the original sentence and the subordinate clause ('occurred') are firmly established in the **past**.
 
• **Past Perfect**: Uses **Had + V3** (e.g., 'Had the panel evaluated...'). This tense represents an action **completed** before another past action, which contradicts the **simultaneous continuous nature** of the original sentence.
 
• **Active Voice** emphasizes the **agent** performing the action, while **Passive Voice** emphasizes the **recipient** of the action or the action itself.
 
 
</ul

questions.question:
Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into active voice?
The solution is known to everybody in the class.

options.text: Everybody in the class is knowing the solution.
Everybody in the class knew the solution.
Everybody in the class knows the solution.
Everybody in the class has known the solution.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Everybody in the class knows the solution.**__.

**__Key Points__**

__

• The original sentence is in the **Passive Voice**. The structure used is **Object + is/am/are + Past Participle (V3) + to + Agent**.

• To convert a sentence from **Passive to Active Voice**, the agent of the action (the person or thing doing the action) must become the **Subject**. In this case, **everybody in the class** becomes the subject.

• The verb **is known** indicates that the sentence is in the **Simple Present Tense**. Therefore, the active verb must also be in the **Simple Present Tense** (V1 or V1+s/es).

• The word **everybody** is a **singular indefinite pronoun**. According to the rules of **Subject-Verb Agreement**, a singular subject requires a singular verb, which is **knows**.

• The receiver of the action, **the solution**, shifts from the subject position in the passive voice to the **Direct Object** position in the active voice.

 **Additional Information__**

• **Stative Verbs**:

• Verbs like **know**, **believe**, and **own** describe a state rather than a continuous action.

• These verbs are typically not used in the **Present Continuous Tense**. Therefore, a construction like **is knowing** is generally considered grammatically incorrect in standard English.

• **Tense Changes**:

• Changing the tense during voice conversion is incorrect. Using **knew** (Simple Past) or **has known** (Present Perfect) alters the temporal context of the original statement.

• Voice conversion only changes the **emphasis** (from the receiver to the doer) while keeping the **tense** constant.

</ul

questions.question:
In the given question, a sentence is divided into four parts and given in the alternatives (A), (B), (C), and (D). There is an error in one part. Choose the alternative containing that part of the sentence that has the error. Choosing the alternative with the error will be the answer.
It was very stupid about the boy to have spent five thousand rupees on that dictionary.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 2**.

 

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• The error in the sentence lies in the use of the preposition **about** in the second part.
 
• When an adjective is used to describe the **nature**, **character**, or **behavior** of a person in the structure **'It + be + adjective + preposition + person + to-infinitive'**, the correct preposition to use is **of**.
 
• Adjectives that typically follow this pattern include **stupid**, **kind**, **nice**, **clever**, **polite**, and **generous**.
 
• The phrase should correctly read as **'stupid of the boy to'** because it describes the boy's action/character.
 
• Thus, the part containing the error is **'stupid about the boy to'**.

Therefore, the correct answer is **stupid about the boy to**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *'It was very **stupid of the boy to** have spent five thousand rupees on that dictionary.'*

 

**Additional Information__**

 
• **'It was very'** – This is a grammatically correct introductory phrase for this type of sentence structure.
 
• **'have spent five thousand'** – The use of the **perfect infinitive** ('to have spent') is correct here as it refers to an action that took place before the time referred to by the main verb ('was').
 
• **'rupees on that dictionary'** – The verb **spend** is correctly paired with the preposition **on** when indicating what the money was exchanged for.
</ul

questions.question:

Sebastian always boasts ____ his European descent.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is '**of**'. **__Key Points__** __ 
• The verb **boast** means to speak with excessive pride and self-satisfaction about one's achievements, possessions, or abilities. 
• In English grammar, the verb **boast** is typically followed by the **preposition** **of** or **about** to indicate the subject of the pride. 
• The phrase **boast of something** is a standard idiomatic construction. In this sentence, **Sebastian** is speaking proudly of his **European descent**. 
• **Options 1, 3**, and **4** are grammatically incorrect because these prepositions do not collocate with the verb **boast** in this context. Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 2**. **Complete Sentence:** *'Sebastian always **boasts of**__ his European descent.'* **__Additional Information__** 
• **Option 1: 'with'** is incorrect; we do not use **with** to specify what is being boasted about. 
• **Option 3: 'at'** is incorrect; the preposition **at** is used for locations or specific points in time, not with the verb **boast**. 
• **Option 4: 'for'** is incorrect; while **for** can indicate purpose, it does not function as the required preposition for the verb **boast**. </ul

questions.question:
A part of the following sentence is underlined. Choose the option that can replace the underlined part to improve the sentence. If you feel Options A, B, or C do not improve the sentence, then choose Option D: "No improvement required."
You need to come to terms with the fact that you have lost your chance and there's no going back.

options.text: come at terms of the fact
come on terms with the facts
come in terms to the fact

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**No improvement required**__.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• The underlined phrase **'come to terms with'** is a fixed **idiomatic expression** in English which means to gradually **accept** a sad or difficult situation or to find a way to live with it.
 
• This idiom follows a strict **syntactic structure** consisting of the verb **'come'**, the prepositional phrase **'to terms'**, and the preposition **'with'**. Any deviation from these specific prepositions results in an **ungrammatical** or **non-idiomatic** construction.
 
• In the sentence provided, the object of acceptance is **'the fact'**, referring to the specific situation of losing a chance. The use of the **definite article** 'the' before the singular noun 'fact' is logically and grammatically sound because it identifies the **propositional content** that follows (that you have lost your chance).
 
• Because the original sentence correctly utilizes the **standard idiom** and maintains **proper prepositional usage**, it does not require any stylistic or grammatical changes. The integrity of the **clause structure** and the **semantic meaning** are both intact.

 **Additional Information__**

 
• Analysis of incorrect prepositional combinations:
 
 
• **'Come at terms of'**: This is incorrect because **'at terms'** is not a recognized phrase for acceptance; **'at'** usually denotes a specific location or point in time, and **'of'** fails to show the relational bond required by the idiom.
 
• **'Come on terms with'**: Although the phrase **'on good terms'** exists to describe a friendly relationship, it cannot substitute **'to terms'** when describing the psychological process of **resignation** or acceptance.
 
• **'Come in terms to'**: This is often confused with **'in terms of'** (meaning regarding), but **'in terms'** cannot be paired with the verb **'come'** to convey acceptance. Furthermore, **'terms'** must be followed by **'with'** to correctly link to the situation being accepted.
 
 
 
• The word **'terms'** in this context relates to **'conditions'** or **'provisions'**, suggesting that the person has reached a state where they can coexist with the **harsh conditions** of their reality.
</ul

questions.question: What does the text say makes material help inadequate in removing misery?
